newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Sparks still seen for Russian Gazprom, state.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sparks still seen for Russian Gazprom, state.

text.p: Russia's Gazprom will see sparks in its relationship with the government in the future, but analysts were divided on Monday over how volatile the situation could become for the world's largest gas company.

Energy specialists, commenting on RAO Gazprom's annual shareholders' session on Saturday, said the natural gas monoply avoided major issues, including the role of one of Russia's most powerful companies in the economy.
That could mean Russia's single biggest corporate tax payer would either build an uneasy truce with the cabinet or resist government efforts to squeeze it for cash.

Gazprom, one of the least successful companies in getting customers to pay but one the state needs to finance reforms, has 34 percent of world gas reserves, 27 percent of annual global output and accounts for a fifth of Europe's gas supply.

"We have to realise two things. The debate between Gazprom and the government is going to continue," said Jonathan Stern, vice-president of London-based Gas Strategies. But he added, "the fireworks we may have expected did not happen, and that means the relationship may have stabilised."

But other analysts had different views on where Gazprom, which accounts for eight percent of gross domestic product and a quarter of Russia's annual tax receipts, stood in its dispute with the state on how much tax it should pay and restructuring.

"I don't think they reached some kind of truce," said analyst Sergei Glazer of Salomon Bros in London. "I was expecting some sort of discussion of Gazprom's position in the Russian economy, and we did not get this. It means the problems are still in effect and will continue."

Gazprom appears to have increased its influence in government by electing reformist First Deputy Finance Minister Alexei Kudrin and reappointing a top member of President Boris Yeltsin's administrative apparatus to its board.
But the new members can also be seen as the government extending its arm into the company's management.
Failure of commercial bank Uneximbank, which holds 4.08 percent of Gazprom, to win a seat was a sideshow to the larger drama of whether Gazprom could smooth over ties with the state.

Alexander Kazakov, Gazprom's reelected board chairman and deputy head of Yeltin's administration, said on Saturday "you don't have to be from the provinces to see the passions around this company are not going to die down...I'd like to ask for more state trust in Gazprom."
Gazprom Chief Executive Officer Rem Vyakhirev also acknowledged the company's tough patches with the government, which was once an unquestioning, hands-off supporter.

"The signs are clear that Gazprom is going to come under increasing pressure from the government to change the way that it operates," wrote Stephen O'Sullivan, oil and gas director at MC Securities, in a recent research note.
But Gazprom, which paid the equivalent of $608 million in tax arrears to cover Yeltsin's promises to pensioners, could not afford to empty its pockets each time the Kremlin needed cash.
"I don't think Gazprom will be able to pay up the next time they're pressed for this kind of money," Glazer said. "They're reaching the limits of debt capacity."
Gazprom has fallen $2.5 billion behind in tax payments because domestic customers, only half of which actually pay for supplies, owe it $12.5 billion.

Analysts said changes to Gazprom's charter putting the securities watchdog in charge of a total nine-percent stake available to foreigners and requiring company approval for single-group deals of more than three percent would reinforce Gazprom's two-tier share structure.
Vyakhirev said the company has had problems in tracking trade in its whopping 23.67 billion shares, including a nightmare with counterfeiters in the city of Tver.
Gazprom's domestic shares are available only to Russian buyers. Foreigners can buy London-listed American Depositary Receipts, which trade above the home shares.
